extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism, mass communication, and media studies; journalism instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and factors that shape which sources and story material journalists select and how extramedia actors (sources, PR, interest groups, advertisers, government) influence news content. Focuses on practical newsroom constraints and strategic behaviors of external actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source availability / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations' regular office hours, full-time staff, and reachable offices make them easier for journalists to access than private individuals (who may be reachable only briefly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because organizations are easier to contact (secretaries, predictable hours), journalists are more likely to use organizational sources when time or access is limited. Example: airlines have press staffs and can time releases before deadlines; small citizens groups may operate from a home with an answering machine and be hard to reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic or political power of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with economic or political power are more likely to influence news reports than those who lack power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big businesses and politically powerful actors can push their side of the story (hire PR, time releases, threaten advertisers). This power imbalance affects which perspectives dominate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information subsidies (usability / cost / convenience of supplied information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources that provide usable information that is easier and cheaper to use (press releases, prepared statements) function as 'information subsidies' and are more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gandy's concept of 'information subsidies' explains why press releases and PIO materials often become the raw material for stories—because they reduce journalists' time and resource costs. Example: many stories begin from press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints and newsroom efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' available time (e.g., wire service deadlines, broadcast schedules) shapes source selection and reliance on easily available sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under stringent time pressure, reporters (especially wire reporters) rely on official activities and a narrow range of sources. This can produce reliance on single-source accounts or official releases rather than extensive independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived credibility / authority of official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and editors often believe that official sources (government, police) have important things to say and tend to accept official statements as factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewing officials concentrates on authoritative voices and can eliminate the perceived need to double- and triple-check facts; this expediency affects what is reported and how it is framed. Studies show reporters often prefer government sources even when technical experts might be more informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source motivations and vested interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources often supply information that serves their organizational or personal interests (e.g., police publicize crime to bolster budgets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition that sources have 'vested interests' helps explain why they supply certain kinds of information and how that shapes the news agenda and framing. Journalists must consider these motives when evaluating source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source personality and communicative traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A source's personality—extroversion, assertiveness, accessibility, quotability, and perceived credibility—affects a source's prominence (frequency of mention) and dominance (being quoted rather than reported about).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies suggest extroverted or assertive actors get more front-page play. Quotable, accessible sources are easier to use in sound bites and leads; however, some studies find visibility not strongly related to seniority or official roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the news event (human interest vs. issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The event type influences whether individual or organizational sources are used; human-interest stories tend to produce more individual sources and sound bites, while issue/legislative coverage skews to officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories involve people over time (kidnappings, hijackings), journalists have more opportunity to locate and use individuals; when covering policy debates or official business, official sources often dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic location and distance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations located far from an event's location tend to rely primarily on official sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance constrains reporters' ability to access on-the-ground individuals and increases dependence on official statements or wire copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymous / confidential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Some official or insider sources provide information but do not want to be personally identified ('a high government source'); they may use anonymity to test ideas or provide background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential sources can supply valuable background or trial balloons but raise tradeoffs about verification and transparency. Journalists use anonymous sourcing for reasons including protection of sources and obtaining otherwise unavailable information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying, misinformation, and the need for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources may withhold information or deliberately mislead; journalists must sift conflicting reports to produce accurate and complete news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include attorneys who admit to misleading reporters. Because liars seldom confess, verification practices and skepticism are critical—yet may be undermined by time pressure and reliance on official or convenient sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential and political actors' media management / agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. presidents and other political actors can 'create the news' and orchestrate encounters to set public-political discourse terms and emphasize agenda items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political actors benefit from being inherently newsworthy and can time or stage events (press conferences, radio addresses) to dominate coverage. Reagan is cited as an effective manager who orchestrated encounters to shape coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest group tactics to influence media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups lobby, issue guidelines, criticize media, mount boycotts of advertisers, and design campaigns to change coverage or program choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American Bar Association 'fair trial-free press' guidelines; American Family Association letters urging boycotts of advertisers; groups lobbying for content regulation. Interest groups can put media criticism on the news agenda and pressure revisions in media practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations campaigns' direct and indirect influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations activities (press releases, paid ads, staged events) affect media content directly via coverage of PR materials and indirectly by drawing journalists' attention to issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR can be cost-effective for resource-poor groups; PR materials sometimes become news. Evidence on PR's overall influence is mixed: some studies show heavy use of PIO materials; others show limited effects beyond news value. Examples: Kodak ad in Columbia Journalism Review, Barry Commoner's radio spot that generated free ABC coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudoevents and manufactured news
rubrics_metrics.description: Events planned primarily to be reported—'pseudoevents'—are planted, arranged for media convenience, have ambiguous relation to reality, and are often intended to be self-fulfilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boorstin's four properties describe a pseudoevent: not spontaneous; planted for reproduction; relation to reality ambiguous; usually self-fulfilling. Interest groups and PR practitioners design pseudoevents (demonstrations, staged press moments) because they reliably attract coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and revenue influences on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Television and other media must satisfy both audiences and advertisers; advertising markets and sponsor preferences can influence program choices and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network executives acknowledge advertisers are 'always taken into account.' Advertisers' attitudes can shape programming decisions; interest groups may pressure advertisers (boycotts) to change content. The economic structure of media thus constrains editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR industry structure and trends affecting influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Trends such as consolidation of ownership among large PR firms and increasing internationalization change how PR operates and its capacity to influence media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The growth of PR conglomerates (WPP Group, Omnicom) and their global reach alter the resources and tactics available to shape news agendas; this structural context affects how journalists encounter and respond to PR materials.
